\section[el medio ambiente]{el medio ambiente — the environment}

\label{lesson:ES-C607-medio-ambiente}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the charity, then the Spanish for to take part.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el medio ambiente}
\textbf{el medio ambiente} — \textquotedblleft{}the environment\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Hay que cuidar el medio ambiente.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We have to look after the environment.}
\end{quote}

Also written \emph{medioambiente}; the adjective is \emph{medioambiental}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{el medio ambiente} is built on \emph{medio}, inherited from Latin \emph{medius} 'middle', and \emph{ambiente}, from Latin \emph{ambiens} 'going round', from \emph{ambire} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el medio ambiente}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el medio ambiente}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el medio ambiente}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the charity, then the Spanish for to take part, then say \emph{el medio ambiente} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does el medio ambiente mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The environment\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el consumo]{el consumo — the consumption}

\label{lesson:ES-C607-consumo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to take part, then the Spanish for the environment.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el consumo}
\textbf{el consumo} — \textquotedblleft{}the consumption\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El consumo de agua es muy alto.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Water consumption is very high.}
\end{quote}

\emph{La sociedad de consumo} — the consumer society.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{consumo} is built on \emph{consumir}, a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{consumere} 'to use up', from \emph{sumere} 'to take' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el consumo}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el consumo}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el consumo}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to take part, then the Spanish for the environment, then say \emph{el consumo} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does el consumo mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The consumption\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[consumir]{consumir — to consume, to use}

\label{lesson:ES-C607-consumir}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the environment, then the Spanish for the consumption.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: consumir}
\textbf{consumir} — \textquotedblleft{}to consume, to use\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Este coche consume poca gasolina.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{This car uses little petrol.}
\end{quote}

Regular -ir verb.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{consumir} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{consumere} 'to use up', built from \emph{con} and \emph{sumere} 'to take' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[el recurso]{el recurso — the resource; the appeal}

\label{lesson:ES-C607-recurso}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the consumption, then the Spanish for to consume.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el recurso}
\textbf{el recurso} — \textquotedblleft{}the resource; the appeal\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El agua es un recurso limitado.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Water is a limited resource.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Recursos humanos} — human resources. In law, an appeal.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{recurso} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{recursus} 'a return, a running back', built on \emph{currere} 'to run' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[la medida]{la medida — the measure, the step; the size}

\label{lesson:ES-C607-medida}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to consume, then the Spanish for the resource.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la medida}
\textbf{la medida} — \textquotedblleft{}the measure, the step; the size\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El gobierno tomó nuevas medidas.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The government took new measures.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Tomar medidas} — to take steps. \emph{A medida que} — as.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{medida} is built on \emph{medir}, which is inherited from spoken Latin \emph{metire}, Latin \emph{metiri} 'to measure' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la medida}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la medida}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to consume, then the Spanish for the resource, then say \emph{la medida} again
